**Subject: Papa’s building on rue Saint-Hubert — stop this sale and call me**

Denis,

I have started this email several times. I am so angry that I do not trust myself to write it the way I would normally speak to you, so I am going to be as clear as I can.

What you have done with Papa’s building is not acceptable. Putting it on the market behind my back, without even calling me first, is one of the most disrespectful things you have ever done to me.

Thursday morning at six o’clock, while I was shaping the baguettes, a photographer from the agency walked into my shop with his camera. He told me that Mr. Denis had told him I was okay with it. Karine had to calm me down. That is how I found out: from a stranger standing in my bakery at six in the morning, acting as if photographing my workplace and the building where I have spent 31 years of my life was an ordinary appointment I had agreed to.

Afterwards, I found the listing myself on Centris. There it was, with an agent, priced at $1,150,000.

Do you understand how humiliating that was? A photographer knew what was happening before I did. Strangers could see the listing before I even knew it existed. Meanwhile, I was downstairs working, as I have been almost every morning for more than three decades, completely unaware that my own brother was preparing to sell the building over my head.

You did not call me. You did not write to me. You did not give me the basic respect of hearing it from you. You let an agent move everything forward and left me to discover it like a stranger. The way you handled this was cowardly. I am not going to soften that word just to make this email easier for you to read.

After Maman’s funeral, you called me and said, “No rush. We’ll decide together.”

Together, Denis.

Those were your words. I believed you. I believed that after losing Maman, we would at least be honest with each other about Papa’s building. I did not think “together” meant you would make arrangements with an agent in secret while I continued paying my rent and running my business.

Papa bought that three-storey building on rue Saint-Hubert in 1979. The bakery is downstairs, with the two apartments above. Since Maman died in February 2026 and the estate was settled in August, it belongs half to you and half to me. I understand that your half is yours. I am not pretending otherwise. But this is not some investment property you bought last year with people you barely know. It is Papa’s building, it is my workplace, and now it is something we own together.

I have paid $2,400 a month in rent to the estate, and I have never once been late. In 2019, I paid $38,000 myself for the new roof. I put that money into the building because I believed in its future and in my future there. So please do not speak to me as if I am just a sentimental tenant who does not understand money or responsibility.

And my intention to buy your half is not news to you. I told you on the phone in September that I wanted to buy it. I told you that the caisse had pre-approved me for $410,000. You knew before this listing went up that I was serious. If you thought the amount would not be enough, you could have said so. If you had questions about my financing, you could have asked them. If you wanted an appraisal or wanted to discuss numbers and conditions, we could have done that. Instead, you said nothing to me and went to an agent.

Perhaps because you live in Calgary, the building feels far away to you. Perhaps it has become mostly an address, a value on paper, or a responsibility you no longer want. I am willing to hear that. You are allowed to want something different from what I want. You are allowed to tell me honestly that you need to sell.

But it is not far away for me. I am inside it every morning. My whole working life is there.

My lease runs until 30 April 2027, but that does not make this sale harmless to me. You know as well as I do what can happen when a developer buys a building like this. They can plan to tear it down or turn it into condos. A new owner can eventually double my rent or make it impossible for me to stay. My bakery cannot survive that. A lease date does not give me a new location, a new clientele, or another 31 years to build everything again.

This is not only about emotion. It is business too. I have six employees. I have customers who have been coming to me for decades. There are people whose parents bought bread here before them and whose children know this shop. Every morning, real work happens inside those walls. You cannot reduce all of that to a listing price and then accuse me of being too sentimental because I object.

And yes, of course I am emotional. Papa bought that building. Maman is gone. The bakery has been my life for 31 years. I am not ashamed of caring about it. But my emotions do not cancel out the business facts, and the business facts do not excuse what you did.

You know this place personally, Denis. When we were kids, Papa used to let you sleep in the little room at the back where the flour sacks were kept. You loved it back there. You have your own memories inside that building. You are not some outside investor who found an address on Centris. You know exactly what it means. That is part of why this hurts so much.

I do not believe you are a cruel man, and I am not writing to say that I hate you. I do not hate you. You are my brother, and I do not want this to be the thing that ends our relationship. But you need to understand that I am furious, and that my trust in you has been badly damaged. Do not mistake the fact that this email is controlled for a lack of anger. This is me trying very hard not to let my anger destroy any chance we still have of fixing it.

So here is what I am asking for, in plain words:

1. **Take the building off the market this week.** Stop moving this sale forward behind my back. No more photographers or visits arranged as though I have already agreed. We need to speak directly and agree on a process before anything else happens.

2. **If you refuse to withdraw the listing, then at the absolute minimum, give me a written first right to buy your half before you sell to anyone else.** I mean a genuine right of first refusal, with the full information and a real opportunity to act—not a phone call after you have already committed yourself to another buyer.

3. **Call me yourself.** I want an answer by phone, not a text from your wife and not a message passed through the agent. Neither of them stood with me after Maman’s funeral and promised that we would decide together. You did. This conversation is between you and me, and I need to hear your voice.

I am still prepared to discuss buying your half seriously and fairly. I am not asking you to give it to me or to disregard your own interests. I am asking for honesty, respect, and a real chance. If your position has changed since September, tell me. If you have another plan, explain it to me. If there is something you need from me in order to make a purchase possible, say it directly.

What you cannot expect is for me to quietly accept this because we are family. Family does not mean I have to swallow whatever you decide. If anything, being my brother means you owed me more honesty, not less.

I do not want to lose my brother over this building. But I also will not stand by quietly and risk losing Papa’s building, my bakery, and everything I have spent 31 years building because you chose an agent over a difficult conversation with me.

Take the listing down this week, or give me the written first right to buy. Then call me. I will answer. I am ready to talk about a real solution, but I am not ready to pretend that what you did was acceptable.

I love you. I am furious with you. Both things are true. What happens next depends a great deal on whether you are finally willing to speak to me directly.

[Your name]
